chapter_summary:
As data engineers, our responsibility extends beyond just building pipelines; we must also ensure they run efficiently, reliably, and predictably. This chapter introduces you to the essential tools and techniques for monitoring your Databricks workloads and understanding their performance characteristics. Effective monitoring is the first line of defense against data quality issues, processing delays, and unexpected costs. Without it, you're operating in the dark, unable to proactively address problems before they impact downstream consumers or business operations.

The Databricks platform provides a rich set of built-in monitoring capabilities. Your primary interface for high-level monitoring will be the Databricks Workspace UI. Here, you can navigate to the "Jobs" section to view the status of all your scheduled and triggered jobs, including their run history, duration, and success/failure status. Clicking into a specific job run provides detailed logs from the driver and executors, allowing you to pinpoint errors or understand execution flow. Similarly, the "Clusters" section offers insights into the health, utilization, and events of your compute resources. You can see which notebooks or jobs are running on a cluster, its current CPU/memory usage, and even restart or terminate it if necessary. For interactive development, the "Query History" tab is invaluable, showing every query executed, its duration, and the user who ran it, which can be crucial for debugging slow queries or identifying resource-intensive operations.

Beyond the high-level UI, Apache Spark, the engine underpinning Databricks, offers the Spark UI, a powerful web interface for deep-dive analysis of individual Spark applications. When a Spark job is running or has recently completed, you can access its Spark UI directly from the Databricks job or cluster details page. The Spark UI is organized into several tabs: "Jobs," "Stages," "Tasks," "Storage," "Environment," and "Executors." The "Stages" tab is particularly useful as it breaks down the execution into logical steps, showing the duration of each stage, input/output sizes, and shuffle read/write metrics. If you see a stage taking an unusually long time, it often points to data skew, inefficient joins, or excessive shuffling. The "Executors" tab provides a summary of resource usage per executor, including CPU time, memory, and garbage collection activity. A common mistake is to only look at the overall job status. Instead, delve into the Spark UI to understand *why* a job failed or was slow. For instance, high "shuffle spill" in the "Stages" tab indicates that Spark is writing intermediate data to disk because it ran out of memory, which is a major performance bottleneck.

Logging is another critical component of monitoring. Databricks automatically captures Spark event logs and driver/executor logs. However, you should also implement custom logging within your Python or Scala code to track application-specific events, progress, and debugging information. Using Python's standard `logging` module or Scala's `log4j` directly within your notebooks or job code allows you to emit messages that appear in the Databricks job logs. For example, logging the number of records processed at different stages of a pipeline can help verify data integrity and track progress.

```python
import logging

# Configure basic logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format='%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s')

def process_data(df):
    logging.info(f"Starting data processing for {df.count()} records.")
    # Simulate some processing
    processed_df = df.filter("value > 10")
    logging.info(f"Filtered to {processed_df.count()} records. Continuing transformation...")
    return processed_df

# Example usage in a Databricks notebook
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("MonitoringExample").getOrCreate()
data = [(1, "A", 5), (2, "B", 12), (3, "C", 8), (4, "D", 15)]
columns = ["id", "name", "value"]
df = spark.createDataFrame(data, columns)

result_df = process_data(df)
result_df.display()
logging.info("Data processing completed successfully.")
```

For more advanced monitoring and alerting, Databricks integrates with various external tools. While Databricks itself offers basic alerting on job success/failure, for richer metrics and custom alerts, you might export logs and metrics to services like Splunk, Datadog, or Azure Monitor/AWS CloudWatch. These platforms can ingest Databricks diagnostic logs, allowing you to build custom dashboards, set thresholds for metrics like cluster utilization or job duration, and trigger notifications via email, Slack, or PagerDuty. For instance, you could set an alert if a daily ETL job takes more than twice its average execution time, indicating a potential issue.

A common mistake is to ignore the "Event Logs" section in the Spark UI. This log provides a chronological record of all events in your Spark application, from driver startup to task completion and garbage collection. It's an invaluable resource for understanding the exact sequence of operations and identifying where delays or failures occurred. Another pitfall is not setting up proper logging levels. During development, `DEBUG` or `INFO` might be appropriate, but for production, you might want to switch to `INFO` or `WARNING` to avoid overwhelming logs with unnecessary detail, while still capturing critical events. Always ensure your logging is consistent and provides enough context to troubleshoot without being excessively verbose.

screens.title: Monitoring Databricks Workloads and Performance
screens.subtitle: Use the Databricks UI, the Spark UI, and logging to find and fix reliability and performance issues.

narration.text: Monitoring is how you turn pipelines from opaque processes into observable systems. In this chapter you will learn to use the Databricks Workspace UI for high-level visibility, open the Spark UI for deep diagnostics, and add targeted logging and alerts so problems are discovered before they affect downstream consumers. You'll see concrete examples: how a job run page reveals driver errors, how the Stages tab points to shuffle or skew issues, and how a simple logging call can make debugging trivial. We'll also cover common mistakes, like collecting large datasets to the driver, and practical mitigations such as distributed aggregations and alert thresholds. By the end you'll understand not just where to look, but what metrics and logs actually mean, how to read garbage collection and shuffle metrics, and how to set a basic alert on job duration. A strong monitoring practice reduces downtime, prevents data-quality regressions, and controls cloud cost. Consider a daily ETL that silently slows by 2x — monitoring helps you spot that trend early and act. Ready to explore the tools and the mindset that make pipelines reliable?

keyIdea.title: Why monitoring matters
keyIdea.text: Monitoring turns guesswork into actionable signals: job status, stage timings, executor health, and logs together help you diagnose and prevent failures and unexpected cost.

screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after completing this chapter

narration.text: These objectives map to concrete monitoring skills you'll use every day. First, you'll learn to navigate the Databricks Workspace UI to inspect Jobs, Clusters, and Query History so you can quickly find failing runs and view basic logs. For example, opening a job run shows driver and executor logs that often contain the exact stack trace you need. Second, you'll interpret Spark UI metrics and event logs to diagnose bottlenecks. Practically, that means reading the Stages tab to spot shuffle spills or data skew. Third, you'll implement custom logging inside notebooks and jobs using standard libraries so your application emits meaningful progress and error messages. A simple logging call that reports record counts at each pipeline stage is extremely helpful in production. Finally, you'll configure basic alerts for critical failures or when durations deviate beyond thresholds. An alert that fires when a daily job takes more than twice its average execution time lets you act before downstream reports break. Each objective emphasizes a skill and a practical outcome: find the cause, verify the fix, and prevent recurrence.

screens.title: Databricks Workspace UI: Jobs, Clusters, and Query History
screens.subtitle: High-level monitoring to find runs, logs, and quick cluster health information

narration.text: The Databricks Workspace UI is your first stop when something goes wrong. It provides high-level listings of Jobs, Clusters, Notebooks, and Query History so you can triage quickly. For example, open the Jobs page to see recent runs, their status, and durations; clicking a run surfaces consolidated logs from the driver and executors. Use the Clusters page to confirm whether a cluster is running, view C P U and memory usage, and see which notebooks or jobs are attached. The Query History tab lists interactive queries with user, duration, and timing information — useful when a single query is causing resource contention. A common misconception is that the workspace UI alone gives full root-cause insight. It doesn't: it tells you where to look and shows aggregated logs, but for stage-level timing and per-task metrics you must open the Spark UI. In practice, combine a quick workspace check to find the run and log lines, then escalate to Spark UI for deep analysis. Think of the workspace UI as your triage tool: it narrows the problem to a run or cluster so subsequent investigation can be focused and efficient.

keyIdea.title: Triage with the Workspace UI
keyIdea.text: Use Jobs and Clusters pages to find failing runs and view surface logs; this narrows where to dive deeper with the Spark UI.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Databricks Workspace UI
Definition

Jobs, Clusters, Query History

The Workspace UI lists runs and cluster health, exposing logs you need for first-pass diagnosis.

Jobs
Run history, durations, success/failure, and links to driver/executor logs for the selected run.
Clusters
Cluster state, CPU/memory metrics, attached notebooks, and restart/terminate controls for operations.
Query History
Interactive query list with duration and user details for debugging slow ad-hoc queries.
Concrete Example
You find a failing nightly ETL. The Jobs page shows several recent failures. Open the latest run and scan the driver log for an exception line that indicates why the job failed—often a stack trace or a custom logging message added in your notebook.
Common mistake

Assuming workspace logs always show per-task metrics. They show aggregated driver/executor output; for per-task timing, use the Spark UI.

Key Takeaway

Start at Workspace UI to locate the run and the logs, then escalate to Spark UI for task-level analysis.

screens.title: The Spark UI: Tabs and What They Tell You
screens.subtitle: Jobs, Stages, Tasks, Executors, Storage and Environment explained

narration.text: The Spark UI is the detailed diagnostic interface for a single Spark application. It organizes information into tabs: Jobs shows the top-level job and the stages it includes; Stages breaks execution into logical steps and reports duration, input/output sizes, and shuffle read/write metrics; Tasks lists individual tasks with timings for each partition; Storage lists cached RDDs and DataFrames; Environment shows configuration and classpaths; and Executors summarizes resource usage per executor. A clear workflow is to open the Stages tab first when a job is slow: stages display shuffle spill counters and input sizes that often reveal data skew or memory pressure. If you find a stage with high spill-to-disk, that indicates intermediate data exceeded memory and was written to disk. A common misconception is to treat total job duration as the diagnostic endpoint. Instead, use stage and task metrics to find which stage or partition takes the longest. For example, if one stage shows a single task with far larger time and input size, you likely have data skew. The Spark UI lets you move from symptom to root cause by making execution visible at multiple granularities.

keyIdea.title: Spark UI workflow
keyIdea.text: Use Stages then Tasks then Executors: stages localize slow work, tasks show partition-level issues, and executors show resource pressure.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Spark UI Overview
Definition

Spark UI Tabs

Jobs
Top-level jobs and links to their stages.
Stages
Breakdown of each stage with shuffle, input/output and duration metrics.
Tasks
Per-task durations and failure reasons for partition-level debugging.
Executors
Memory, CPU, and GC stats for each executor to identify resource pressure.
Example
Imagine a job with a stage that reads a large shuffle. The Stages tab shows high shuffle read/write and large spill counts. That points strongly to memory pressure during shuffle and suggests either increasing executor memory, tuning shuffle partitions, or revising the join strategy to reduce shuffle size.
Misconception

Seeing long GC time may seem like a code issue—often it is configuration or insufficient memory. Check executor memory and spill metrics before rewriting logic.

Key Takeaway

Spark UI provides layered visibility; read Stages first, then use Tasks and Executors to confirm the cause and choose a mitigation.

screens.title: Interpreting Stages: Shuffle, Spill, and Data Skew
screens.subtitle: How to read stage metrics to find common performance bottlenecks

narration.text: When a stage runs slowly, the Stages tab gives you specific metrics to interpret. Key indicators include shuffle read/write sizes, shuffle spill counts, and task duration variance. Shuffle read/write sizes show how much intermediate data moved across the network; large values suggest expensive network input and output. Shuffle spill counts indicate how often intermediate data was written to disk because an executor ran out of memory. High spill is a strong signal that you need either more executor memory, fewer concurrent tasks per executor, or a strategy to reduce intermediate data such as broadcasting smaller tables or increasing shuffle partitions. Data skew appears as large variance in task durations: most tasks finish quickly, but a few take much longer because they process disproportionately large partitions. A concrete example is a join on a column with many nulls and a few hot keys; one partition becomes enormous and slows the stage. A common mistake is overprovisioning compute without addressing skew; better is to redistribute keys or use salting to even partition sizes. After diagnosing, pick the least-invasive fix first and measure the effect in a subsequent run.

keyIdea.title: Stage metrics matter
keyIdea.text: High shuffle sizes and spills point to memory and network pressure; task time variance usually means data skew that needs redistribution.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Stages & Bottlenecks
What to Read

Shuffle, Spill, Task Variance

Shuffle Read/Write
Large network transfer of intermediate data; check if joins or wide operations are moving lots of rows.
Shuffle Spill
Count of times intermediate data spilled to disk because memory was insufficient.
Task Time Variance
Large variance in task durations typically means data skew — a small number of partitions doing most work.
Concrete Scenario
A join on a user ID with a few super-users causes one partition to have millions of rows. Stages show a single task taking far longer than the rest. Diagnosis: data skew. Mitigation: pre-aggregate heavy keys, use salting, or broadcast the smaller table if appropriate.
Pro Tip

Measure partition sizes and task durations to confirm skew before changing cluster size. Fixing the distribution is often cheaper than adding resources.

Key Takeaway

Read shuffle and spill metrics first; if task times vary greatly, suspect skew and address data distribution before scaling up compute.

screens.title: Executors and Driver: Memory, CPU, and Garbage Collection
screens.subtitle: Using the Executors tab to diagnose resource pressure and driver OOMs

narration.text: Executors and the driver are the processes that actually execute your Spark tasks. The Executors tab summarizes C P U time, memory used, and garbage collection for each executor. Driver-related issues often appear as out-of-memory errors on the driver process when too much data is brought to the driver, for example by using collect or toPandas. When diagnosing, look for two patterns: sustained high memory usage or repeated GC spikes. High memory and frequent GC usually mean the process is thrashing and not making forward progress; possible fixes include increasing executor memory, decreasing parallelism per executor, or reducing in-memory data size by checkpointing or writing intermediate results to storage. A common mistake is to assume that increasing the number of executors always solves the problem. If the driver is the bottleneck because it is collecting data, adding executors won't help; instead change the code to avoid collect or to use distributed aggregations. For production, aim for steady memory usage with moderate GC activity rather than frequent long GC pauses. Executors and Driver: Memory, CPU, and Garbage Collection means look for high memory, high gc time, or skewed cpu usage per executor; those indicate memory pressure, gc pauses, or uneven work distribution.. In practical terms, using the executors tab to diagnose resource pressure and driver ooms. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Executor signals
keyIdea.text: Look for high memory, high GC time, or skewed CPU usage per executor; those indicate memory pressure, GC pauses, or uneven work distribution.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Executors & Driver
Definition

Memory, CPU, GC Metrics

The Executors tab shows per-executor metrics: memory used, max memory, CPU time, tasks completed, and garbage collection time. The driver also appears here and is special—driver OOMs often mean too much data was collected to the driver process.
Memory Used
Compare used vs available memory to find pressure points.
GC Time
Long GC pauses reduce throughput and signal memory thrashing.
Concrete Example
A job fails with a driver OutOfMemoryError after calling collect on a large DataFrame. Executors may look healthy, but the driver shows memory exhaustion and long GC. The fix is to avoid collect and perform a distributed aggregation or write results to storage.
Common mistake

Adding more executors when the driver is the bottleneck will not solve driver OOMs. Change code to keep work distributed.

Key Takeaway

Use executor metrics to decide between configuration changes and code changes. Driver issues often require code-level fixes.

screens.title: Custom Logging in Notebooks and Jobs
screens.subtitle: Add structured log messages so job logs are actionable

narration.text: Custom logging gives context that system logs cannot. Emitting INFO or ERROR messages inside your code lets you record important checkpoints like record counts, input sources, and transformation milestones. Use Python's standard logging module or Scala's log4j within notebooks and job code. For example, a logging. info call before and after a filter shows how many records were processed and helps verify transformations without scanning data. Put meaningful context in messages: job id, dataset partition, and stage name. A common misconception is that more logs are always better. Excessive DEBUG logs in production make it hard to find relevant errors and increase storage costs. Instead, log key state transitions at INFO and reserve DEBUG for short-lived development runs. Also, ensure logs are searchable by including consistent keys and formats. When run on Databricks, these custom logs appear in the driver logs and can be viewed in the run's Logs tab. Use structured text or key=value pairs so external monitoring tools can parse them for dashboards and alerts. Custom Logging in Notebooks and Jobs means log key state transitions at info with context such as record counts and identifiers; avoid noisy debug logs in production.. In practical terms, add structured log messages so job logs are actionable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Meaningful logs
keyIdea.text: Log key state transitions at INFO with context such as record counts and identifiers; avoid noisy DEBUG logs in production.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Custom Logging
Code Example
This Python example shows configuring logging and emitting record counts at key points. These messages appear in the driver's logs for the run.
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format='%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s')

def process_data(df):
  logging.info(f"Starting data processing for {df.count()} records.")
  processed_df = df.filter("value > 10")
  logging.info(f"Filtered to {processed_df.count()} records. Continuing transformation...")
  return processed_df

# Spark session and example usage
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("MonitoringExample").getOrCreate()
Note: code is shown for illustration; in production prefer non-blocking sampling for counts to avoid extra passes.
Best Practices
  • Log key checkpoints (start, end, record counts) at INFO.
  • Keep DEBUG for development runs only to avoid noisy production logs.
  • Include identifiers and consistent keys so logs are parsable by monitoring systems.
Key Takeaway

Meaningful, consistent logging makes job runs traceable and accelerates debugging without drowning you in noise.

screens.title: Hands-on: A Starter Script that Fails by Design
screens.subtitle: Simulate a driver OutOfMemoryError and learn how to find it in the Spark UI

narration.text: A practical exercise helps cement monitoring skills. The starter script intentionally collects a large DataFrame to the driver, a common anti-pattern that triggers an OutOfMemoryError. Run it on a cluster and observe the job in the Databricks Jobs page. When the run fails or slows, open the Spark UI from the job run. In the Stages tab you may see a stage corresponding to the collect call that runs on the driver with large input size and long duration. In Executors you will observe the driver's memory spike or fail. This is an ideal controlled scenario to practice reading the Stages and Executors tabs and to test mitigations. The correct mitigation is not to add more driver memory without understanding root cause; the right fix is to avoid collect and use distributed aggregations or writes. After diagnosing, modify the code to perform an aggregation and write results to distributed storage, then rerun and confirm the Spark UI shows no driver memory pressure. This exercise links the failure mode to a concrete fix you can verify with Spark metrics. Hands-on: A Starter Script that Fails by Design means intentionally reproduce a driver oom with collect to learn how to locate the failing stage and confirm the fix by using distributed aggregations.. In practical terms, simulate a driver outofmemoryerror and learn how to find it in the spark ui. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Fail to learn
keyIdea.text: Intentionally reproduce a driver OOM with collect to learn how to locate the failing stage and confirm the fix by using distributed aggregations.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Starter Script — Fail Fast
Starter Code
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import rand
import logging

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("SparkUIMonitoring").getOrCreate()
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format='%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s')

num_records = 10000000
logging.info(f"Creating a DataFrame with {num_records} records.")
large_df = spark.range(num_records).withColumn("random_value", rand() * 1000)

logging.info("Attempting to collect large DataFrame to driver. This might cause issues.")
try:
  collected_data = large_df.collect()
  logging.info(f"Successfully collected {len(collected_data)} records.")
except Exception as e:
  logging.error(f"Failed to collect data: {e}")
  print(f"Failed to collect data: {e}")

logging.info("Job finished.")
Activity Steps
  1. Run the script on a cluster and observe the job in Databricks Jobs.
  2. Open the Spark UI from the run and inspect Stages and Executors.
  3. Identify the stage tied to collect and confirm driver memory pressure in Executors.
  4. Change collect to a distributed aggregation and re-run to confirm the fix.
Key Takeaway

Reproducing a failure in a controlled way teaches you where the UI points and what concrete code changes remove the root cause.

screens.title: Spark Event Logs and Post‑mortem Analysis
screens.subtitle: Using event logs to understand the exact sequence of application events

narration.text: Spark Event Logs are chronological records of all significant events in a Spark application: job starts, stage completions, task failures, executor additions and removals, and garbage collection events. Event logs are invaluable for post-mortem analysis because they show the sequence in which things happened, enabling you to correlate a spike in GC with a preceding large shuffle or to see the time an executor was lost. A common mistake is to ignore event logs and rely solely on high-level job status. Event logs let you step through the application lifecycle and understand whether a failure was caused by resource churn, transient executor loss, or a deterministic data issue. When you investigate a failure, use event logs to reconstruct the timeline, then inspect the associated stages and tasks to find the offending operation. For systematic analysis, export event logs to external storage or monitoring tools so you can retain history beyond the UI retention period and create searchable records for recurring incidents. Spark Event Logs and Post‑mortem Analysis means use event logs to reconstruct the sequence of failures or slowdowns and correlate resource events with stage and task behavior.. In practical terms, using event logs to understand the exact sequence of application events. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Event logs are chronological proof
keyIdea.text: Use event logs to reconstruct the sequence of failures or slowdowns and correlate resource events with stage and task behavior.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Event Logs
Definition

Spark Event Logs

Event logs record the timeline of driver and executor events and are a primary artifact for post-mortem analysis. They are generated automatically and can be exported for long-term retention.
Why they help
They let you correlate task failures, GC spikes, and executor events with stage progress to find root causes.
What to look for
Executor additions/removals, task failures, long GC, and job/stage start or end times.
Post-mortem Checklist
  • Reconstruct the timeline from event logs.
  • Match GC spikes to preceding large shuffles or stage starts.
  • Look for executor loss or repeated task retries as signs of instability.
Key Takeaway

Event logs are the canonical timeline you use to prove what happened and to plan a fix that prevents recurrence.

screens.title: Alerting and External Integrations
screens.subtitle: Basic alerts plus exporting logs and metrics for richer monitoring

narration.text: Alerting ensures that problems are noticed and acted upon. Databricks provides basic alerting for job success or failure and job duration thresholds, but many teams export logs and metrics to external systems for richer capabilities. For example, sending metrics to Azure Monitor, Datadog, or Splunk lets you build dashboards, set thresholds on cluster utilization or job duration, and trigger notifications via email, Slack, or PagerDuty. A practical alert to set is one that fires when a critical ETL takes more than twice its average runtime. When designing alerts, choose thresholds that minimize noise: too sensitive and teams ignore them, too lax and they miss real incidents. Also include context in alerts: job id, run id, cluster name, and a short summary of observed metrics. A common mistake is relying solely on job failure alerts; many issues manifest as slowdowns rather than outright failures. Track trends and set anomaly or rate-based alerts for sustained deviations. Finally, test alerts by simulating a slow run to ensure downstream notification channels are working. Alerting and External Integrations means alerts should be actionable, include context, and be tuned to avoid noise; export logs/metrics for dashboards and advanced alerting.. In practical terms, basic alerts plus exporting logs and metrics for richer monitoring. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. keyIdea.text: Alerts should be actionable, include context, and be tuned to avoid noise; export logs/metrics for dashboards and advanced alerting.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Alerting & Integrations
Definition

Alerts and Exported Metrics

Basic in-platform alerts on success/failure or duration are useful, but exporting to observability systems provides richer thresholds, trend analysis, and notification routing.
Practical alert
Alert when a daily job’s runtime exceeds twice its historical average to detect regressions quickly.
Export targets
Export logs and metrics to monitoring tools to build dashboards and set advanced alerts.
Checklist
  • Decide which metrics to alert on (job duration, cluster CPU, driver OOM).
  • Include context in alerts (run id, job name, cluster name).
  • Test alert delivery by simulating a threshold breach.
Key Takeaway

Design alerts to be actionable and test them. Export to monitoring systems for trend detection and richer notification options.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Practical Remedies
screens.subtitle: What teams get wrong and simple, practical corrections

narration.text: Teams often make a predictable set of mistakes when monitoring Databricks workloads. First, collecting large datasets to the driver causes driver OOMs; remedy this by using distributed aggregations, writing to distributed storage, or showing only samples. Second, relying on job status alone misses slowdowns; pair job alerts with duration thresholds and trending metrics. Third, ignoring Spark event logs eliminates the causal timeline—retain and inspect event logs for root-cause analysis. Fourth, excessive logging at DEBUG level in production creates noise and storage costs; instead, log concise INFO events and reserve DEBUG for development. For each mistake, the remedy is practical: avoid collect to driver; use Stages and Executors to troubleshoot; export event logs for history; and structure logs for parsing. A good habit is to run a post-incident checklist: reproduce the issue in a controlled run, capture the event logs, identify the offending stage, apply a targeted fix, and add an alert to detect regression. Small, repeatable practices prevent the same incident from recurring. screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Compact definitions you should keep in mind

narration.text: Keep these six concepts available as mental models when you monitor Databricks workloads. Databricks UI is your triage surface for runs, clusters, and quick logs. The Spark UI gives stage, task, and executor metrics for deep diagnostics. Spark Event Logs are chronological records essential for post-mortem analysis. Driver and Executor Logs contain the output of your application and custom logging, and they live in the run's Logs view. Custom Logging means instrumenting code with INFO and ERROR messages that include context like record counts and run identifiers. Alerting involves setting thresholds and exporting metrics so teams are notified of failures or regressions. Together these elements make pipelines observable: triage with the workspace UI, diagnose with Spark UI and event logs, add context with logging, and close the loop with alerts.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Practical Reminders
screens.subtitle: Short rules to apply when monitoring and debugging

narration.text: Keep this short checklist handy when you face an incident. Always locate the run in the Databricks UI first. Then open the Spark UI and inspect Stages for shuffle and spill metrics. Check the Executors tab for memory and GC signals, and read driver logs for custom logging messages or stack traces. If you see a driver OutOfMemoryError, avoid quick scaling—first change the code to keep work distributed. Finally, set alerts on both failures and sustained increases in job duration. These rules reduce downtime and help you choose the right corrective action quickly.
